'''''Brahea edulis''''', the '''Guadalupe palm''' or '''{{lang|es|palma de Guadalupe|italic=no}}''', is a [[Arecaceae|palm]] [[endemic (ecology)|endemic]] to [[Guadalupe Island]], [[Mexico]], although a few stands have been planted elsewhere.<ref name="Garcillan2012">Garcillan, Pedro P., Ernesto Vega, and Carlos Martorell. "[https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Carlos_Martorell/publication/233988606_The_Brahea_edulis_palm_forest_in_Guadalupe_Island_A_North_American_fog_oasis/links/56cf1eb208ae85c823447ebc.pdf The Brahea edulis palm forest in Guadalupe Island: A North American fog oasis?.]" Revista Chilena de Historia Natural 85 (2012): 137–145.</ref> It is a [[fan palm]] which grows {{convert|4.50|to|13|m|0}} tall. It grows on the island between {{convert|400|and|1000|m}} [[above mean sea level]] (ASL),<ref name = ldlletal2003>León de la Luz ''et al.'' (2003)</ref> with this altitudinal zonation producing one of the few fog oases present in [[North America]].<ref name="Garcillan2012" />

==Distribution and habitat==
''Brahea edulis'' is [[endemic (ecology)|endemic]] to [[Guadalupe Island]], [[Mexico]],<ref name="rebman">{{Cite journal|last=Rebman|first=J. P.|last2=Gibson|first2=J.|last3=Rich|first3=K.|date=2016|title=Annotated checklist of the vascular plants of Baja California, Mexico|url=http://sdplantatlas.org/pdffiles/BajaChecklist2016.pdf|journal=San Diego Society of Natural History|volume=45|page=274}}</ref> found in a monospecific grove around 20 hectares in area between {{convert|400|and|1000|m}} ASL on the north end of the island<ref name = ldlletal2003>León de la Luz ''et al.'' (2003)</ref> The scarped terrain, along with the maritime climate of the island, produces one of the few true fog oases in [[North America]]. The mainland [[Baja California desert]] is [[Fog desert|influenced]] by fog, but the effect is greatly diluted by the lack of steep topography. Although the island's rainfall is low, about {{Convert|133|mm|in|abbr=on}} per year, the effect of the fog and the topography produces an environment similar to the [[lomas]] of [[South America]].<ref name="Garcillan2012" />

The entire native population consists of old trees with little successful recruitment for 150 years or so. Until 2007, Guadalupe Island supported a large [[domestic goat|goat]] population (estimated at 100,000 in 1870, and 5,000 in 2000). The presence of these goats prevented regrowth of the native trees, including ''B. edulis'', and as a consequence, the ecosystem was drastically altered: the once verdant island turned into an almost barren rock, with weeds replacing the former forests. Below {{convert|800|–|900|m|abbr=on}} ASL, the palm is essentially the only remaining tree, occurring in a major subpopulation and scattered groups in sheltered locations. Above that, there used to be a band of mixed woodland where the palm was accompanied by [[Island Oak]] and [[Guadalupe Pine]]. This [[habitat]] has now all but disappeared due to the other trees becoming pushed back into higher regions.<ref name="ldlletal2003" />

== Conservation ==
The species was probably declining slowly since the mid-19th century. Its range might even have expanded a bit until the mid-20th century however; part of it was shared with other trees as noted above; especially the pine, which is a towering species that presumably grew in many sites now occupied by the palm. In addition, a forest of [[Guadalupe Cypress]] and [[California Juniper]] shrubland existed in the palm's present range; the cypress forest was eventually destroyed by the goats and the juniper is nowadays completely absent from the island.<ref name="ldlletal2003" />

Although threatened in the wild, ''B. edulis'' is cultivated, especially in [[California]]. In 2001, it was started to fence in patches of habitat on Guadalupe, and the long-envisioned removal of goats was effectively complete by 2005. Some hundreds of Guadalupe Palms remain on their island home today.<ref>Johnson (1988), León de la Luz ''et al.'' (2003)</ref> As regrowth presumably was hindered by the goats eating the saplings rather than the trees having all become old and sterile, it is likely that the palm will eventually recover.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Cris|first1=Isaak|title=Brahea edulis Guadalupe Palm|url=https://www.mypalmshop.nl/Brahea%20edulis|access-date=12 May 2017|date=1 June 2013}}</ref> That it was best able of all Guadalupe tree species to withstand the hordes of goats is evidenced by its present distribution; the other trees – if they survive at all – are limited to higher and less accessible areas.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Maunder|first1=M.|last2=Lyte|first2=B.|last3=Dransfield|first3=J.|last4=Baker|first4=W.|title=The conservation value of botanic garden palm collections|journal=Biological Conservation|date=1 April 2001|volume=98|issue=3|pages=259–271|doi=10.1016/S0006-3207(00)00160-9}}</ref>
